notes.h: Cell injury, adaptation and cell death
notes.body:
Cells under stress first adapt, then suffer reversible injury, and finally irreversible injury and death.

Adaptations
- Hypertrophy: cells enlarge, for example the left ventricle in hypertension.
- Hyperplasia: cells increase in number, for example the endometrium under oestrogen. Pathological hyperplasia can be a soil for cancer.
- Atrophy: cells shrink through reduced synthesis, autophagy and ubiquitin–proteasome breakdown.
- Metaplasia: one mature cell type replaces another, as in Barrett oesophagus (squamous to columnar with goblet cells) or bronchial squamous metaplasia in smokers. It is reversible but can progress to dysplasia.

Causes
Hypoxia and ischaemia, toxins, infection, immune reactions, genetic defects, nutritional imbalance and physical agents. Ischaemia does more damage than hypoxia alone, because metabolites also accumulate.

Mechanisms
- ATP depletion: the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase fails, so Na⁺ and water enter and the cell swells. Glycolysis causes acidosis, and ribosomes detach.
- Mitochondrial damage: the permeability transition pore opens and cytochrome c leaks out.
- Ca²⁺ influx: activates phospholipases, proteases and endonucleases.
- Reactive oxygen species: lipid peroxidation and protein and DNA damage, worsened in ischaemia–reperfusion injury.
- Severe damage to lysosomal and plasma membranes marks the point of no return.

Morphology
- Reversible injury: cell swelling (hydropic change), fatty change, membrane blebs.
- Irreversible injury: pyknosis, karyorrhexis and karyolysis, with membrane rupture releasing troponin, CK or ALT.

Necrosis versus apoptosis
- Necrosis: pathological and affects groups of cells. Cells swell, membranes rupture and inflammation follows.
- Apoptosis: energy-dependent and programmed. Single cells shrink, chromatin condenses and apoptotic bodies are phagocytosed without inflammation. Examples are embryogenesis, deletion of autoreactive lymphocytes and cytotoxic T-cell killing.
- Regulated necrosis also exists: necroptosis (RIPK1/RIPK3/MLKL) and pyroptosis (inflammasome, caspase-1).

Patterns of necrosis
- Coagulative: architecture preserved. Ischaemic infarcts of solid organs other than the brain.
- Liquefactive: brain infarcts and abscesses.
- Caseous: tuberculous granulomas.
- Fat necrosis: enzymatic in acute pancreatitis (saponification), or traumatic in the breast.
- Fibrinoid: vessel walls in vasculitis and malignant hypertension.
- Gangrene is a clinical term: dry (coagulative) or wet (infected, liquefactive).

Applied illustration
In myocardial infarction, myocyte injury stays reversible for roughly the first 20–30 minutes of severe ischaemia, so prompt reperfusion saves muscle. Reperfusion itself adds ROS and Ca²⁺ injury, and coagulative necrosis is not visible by light microscopy for several hours.

Calcification
- Dystrophic: in damaged tissue with normal serum calcium (atheroma, damaged valves).
- Metastatic: in normal tissue with hypercalcaemia or hyperphosphataemia.

Exam pitfalls
- Do not call apoptosis 'necrosis of single cells'.
- Cerebral infarcts are liquefactive.
- Metaplasia is not dysplasia.

Inflammation is a protective response that brings leucocytes and plasma proteins to sites of infection or injury. Its cardinal signs are rubor, tumor, calor and dolor (Celsus), with functio laesa added later.

Acute inflammation: vascular events
- Arteriolar vasodilatation (histamine, prostaglandins, nitric oxide) causes redness and heat.
- Increased permeability, mainly from endothelial contraction in postcapillary venules, produces a protein-rich exudate (specific gravity above 1.020), unlike a transudate.

Neutrophil recruitment
- Rolling, mediated by selectins (E- and P-selectin on endothelium, L-selectin on leucocytes).
- Firm adhesion: integrins (LFA-1, Mac-1) bind ICAM-1.
- Transmigration via PECAM-1.
- Chemotaxis towards C5a, IL-8 (CXCL8), LTB₄ and bacterial peptides.
- Phagocytosis, aided by opsonins (C3b, IgG), with killing by the oxidative burst (NADPH oxidase, then myeloperoxidase making HOCl).
- Leucocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 (CD18) causes recurrent infections without pus and delayed separation of the umbilical cord. Chronic granulomatous disease (NADPH oxidase) causes infections with catalase-positive organisms.

Mediators
- Histamine (mast cells): early permeability.
- Prostaglandins via COX: vasodilatation, pain and fever (PGE₂). This explains NSAID effects.
- Leukotrienes: LTB₄ attracts neutrophils; LTC₄, D₄ and E₄ cause bronchoconstriction.
- TNF, IL-1 and IL-6: fever, hepatic CRP production, neutrophilia.
- Complement: C3a and C5a are anaphylatoxins, C3b opsonises, and C5b–9 forms the membrane attack complex.
- Bradykinin: pain and permeability.

Outcomes and patterns
Acute inflammation can resolve, heal by fibrosis, form an abscess, or become chronic. Morphological patterns are serous (blisters, effusions), fibrinous (pericarditis), suppurative (abscess) and ulcerative.

Chronic inflammation
Inflammation, tissue destruction and attempts at repair happen together. Macrophages, lymphocytes and plasma cells predominate.
- Causes: persistent infection (tuberculosis), prolonged toxic exposure (silica), autoimmunity.
- M1 macrophages, activated by IFN-γ, kill microbes. M2 macrophages, activated by IL-4 and IL-13, promote repair and fibrosis.
- Granulomatous inflammation: epithelioid macrophages, often with multinucleate giant cells, surrounded by lymphocytes and driven by Th1 cytokines (IFN-γ). Caseating granulomas suggest tuberculosis. Non-caseating granulomas occur in sarcoidosis, Crohn disease, foreign bodies and berylliosis.

Systemic effects
Fever, raised CRP and ESR, and leucocytosis: neutrophilia in bacterial infection, lymphocytosis in viral infection, eosinophilia in parasitic and allergic conditions. Long-standing inflammation can cause AA amyloidosis.

Applied illustration
In acute appendicitis, luminal obstruction allows bacterial invasion, and neutrophils infiltrate the muscularis propria. Untreated, it may progress to gangrene and perforation with peritonitis, or be walled off as an appendix mass or abscess.

Exam pitfalls
- Exudate is not transudate.
- A granuloma is not granulation tissue.
- Chronic inflammation is defined by its histological pattern, not just its duration.

Repair happens by regeneration or by scarring, depending on whether the cells can divide and whether the matrix framework survives.

Proliferative capacity
- Labile: surface epithelia, bone marrow.
- Stable (quiescent but can re-enter the cycle): hepatocytes, renal tubular cells, fibroblasts, endothelium.
- Permanent: neurones and cardiac myocytes, which heal by scar or gliosis.
Destroying the framework causes scarring even in stable tissue. Chronic liver injury produces cirrhosis: regenerative nodules surrounded by fibrous septa.

Phases of scar formation
- Haemostasis and inflammation (hours to days): a fibrin clot forms; neutrophils arrive, then macrophages.
- Proliferation (from about day 3): granulation tissue forms, made of new capillaries (VEGF-driven angiogenesis), fibroblasts and loose matrix. Epithelium regenerates over the surface.
- Remodelling (weeks to months): type III collagen is replaced by type I, myofibroblasts contract the wound, and matrix metalloproteinases remodel the matrix.

Mediators
TGF-β is the main fibrogenic cytokine. PDGF and FGF drive fibroblast and endothelial proliferation, and VEGF drives angiogenesis.

Primary versus secondary intention
- Primary: a clean, sutured incision with apposed edges. There is little granulation tissue and a narrow scar.
- Secondary: a large defect with separated edges, such as an ulcer or infected wound. There is abundant granulation tissue, marked contraction and a larger scar.

Factors impairing healing
- Local: infection (the most important), poor blood supply, foreign bodies, movement, pressure, radiation.
- Systemic: diabetes, poor nutrition, glucocorticoids, old age, malignancy.
- Vitamin C is a cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases. Deficiency (scurvy) gives weak collagen, poor healing, bleeding gums and perifollicular haemorrhages. Zinc deficiency and Ehlers–Danlos syndromes also impair healing.

Abnormal repair
- Hypertrophic scar: stays within the wound margins and may regress.
- Keloid: extends beyond the margins, is more common in darker skin, and often recurs after excision.
- Contracture, for example after burns.
- Dehiscence and incisional hernia.
- Organ fibrosis (pulmonary fibrosis, cirrhosis, chronic kidney disease), driven by persistent injury and TGF-β.

Specific tissues
- Fracture: haematoma, soft callus, woven-bone hard callus, then remodelling to lamellar bone.
- Myocardial infarct: collagen scar by about 6–8 weeks.
- Brain: astrocytic gliosis.
- Peripheral nerve: Wallerian degeneration, then regrowth along Schwann cell tubes at about 1 mm per day.

Applied illustration
A sutured incision shows neutrophils at 24 hours, macrophages and granulation tissue by days 3–5, and bridging collagen by the end of the first week. When sutures come out at about a week, the wound has only about 10% of normal strength, rising to about 70–80% by three months. Patients are therefore told to avoid heavy lifting.

Exam pitfalls
- Granulation tissue is not a granuloma.
- Scar strength never fully returns to normal.
- Cardiac muscle is permanent, not stable.

A thrombus is a solid mass of blood constituents formed within an intact vessel during life.

Virchow's triad
- Endothelial injury: dominant in arteries and the heart, for example plaque rupture or endocardium after infarction.
- Abnormal flow: stasis (deep veins, the left atrium in atrial fibrillation, aneurysms) or turbulence.
- Hypercoagulability, either inherited or acquired.
- Inherited: factor V Leiden (resistance to activated protein C, the commonest inherited cause in Europeans), prothrombin G20210A, and deficiency of protein C, protein S or antithrombin.
- Acquired: surgery and immobility, cancer, pregnancy and the postpartum period, combined oral contraception, antiphospholipid syndrome, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, nephrotic syndrome.

Arterial versus venous thrombi
- Arterial thrombi are platelet-rich ('white'), form at plaque rupture, and are prevented mainly with antiplatelet drugs.
- Venous thrombi are rich in red cells and fibrin ('red'), form in stasis, and are treated with anticoagulants (heparins, DOACs, warfarin).
- Lines of Zahn show a thrombus formed in flowing blood, which distinguishes it from a post-mortem clot.
- A thrombus may resolve by fibrinolysis, propagate, organise and recanalise, or embolise.

Embolism
- Thromboembolism: about 95% of pulmonary emboli arise from deep vein thrombosis in the legs. Systemic emboli usually come from the heart (atrial fibrillation, mural thrombus, vegetations) and lodge in the brain, gut, kidney, spleen or limbs. A patent foramen ovale allows paradoxical embolism.
- Fat embolism: 24–72 hours after a long-bone fracture, with hypoxaemia, confusion and a petechial rash.
- Amniotic fluid embolism: sudden collapse with DIC around delivery.
- Gas embolism: decompression sickness or iatrogenic air.

Infarction
Infarction is ischaemic necrosis from loss of arterial supply or venous drainage.
- White (anaemic) infarcts occur in solid organs with end-arterial supply: heart, kidney, spleen.
- Red (haemorrhagic) infarcts occur with a dual supply (lung, intestine), venous occlusion (testicular torsion), loose tissue, or reperfusion.
- Infarcts are usually wedge-shaped, with the occluded vessel at the apex. Extent depends on collateral supply, how fast the occlusion develops, how vulnerable the tissue is (neurones die within minutes), and blood oxygen content.

Applied illustration
Ms Patel, 34, develops a swollen calf after a long-haul flight while taking combined oral contraception, combining stasis and hypercoagulability. A large saddle embolus at the pulmonary bifurcation can cause acute right ventricular failure and death. Smaller emboli cause infarction only sometimes, typically when the bronchial supply is also compromised (for example in left heart failure). The infarcts are then haemorrhagic. NICE NG158 recommends the two-level Wells score, D-dimer and imaging for suspected DVT or PE.

Exam pitfalls
- A thrombus is not a clot.
- Most pulmonary emboli do not cause infarction.
- Brain infarcts are liquefactive.
- Prevent arterial thrombosis with antiplatelets; treat venous thrombosis with anticoagulants.

A neoplasm is an abnormal mass of tissue whose growth is excessive, uncoordinated with surrounding tissue, and continues after the stimulus has gone. Clonality distinguishes it from hyperplasia.

Benign versus malignant
- Benign tumours: usually well differentiated, slow-growing, often encapsulated and expansile. They do not metastasise, but can cause harm through pressure, position or hormone secretion (for example a pituitary adenoma).
- Malignant tumours: invade and can metastasise. They show pleomorphism, a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, abnormal mitoses and necrosis.

Nomenclature
- Benign: adenoma, papilloma, lipoma, leiomyoma.
- Malignant: carcinoma (epithelial: adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma), sarcoma (mesenchymal), leukaemia and lymphoma.
- Melanoma, mesothelioma and seminoma are malignant despite the '-oma'.
- Hamartoma: disorganised native tissue. Choristoma: normal tissue in the wrong place.

Dysplasia and carcinoma in situ
Dysplasia is disordered growth with atypia and loss of maturation. Carcinoma in situ is full-thickness dysplasia with an intact basement membrane. It cannot metastasise until it invades.

Carcinogenesis
Cancer develops through many steps, accumulating genetic and epigenetic changes. The colorectal adenoma–carcinoma sequence (Fearon and Vogelstein, 1990) runs from APC loss, through KRAS activation, to TP53 loss. Hanahan and Weinberg's hallmarks (2000; updated 2011 and 2022) include sustained proliferative signalling, evasion of growth suppressors, resistance to cell death, replicative immortality, angiogenesis, invasion and metastasis, altered metabolism and immune evasion.

Carcinogens
- Chemical: tobacco polycyclic hydrocarbons, aflatoxin (liver), aromatic amines (bladder), asbestos (mesothelioma).
- Radiation: UV (skin) and ionising radiation.
- Viruses: high-risk HPV 16 and 18 (E6 targets p53, E7 targets Rb), EBV, HBV, HCV, HHV-8 and HTLV-1.
- Bacteria: Helicobacter pylori (gastric adenocarcinoma, MALT lymphoma).

Invasion and metastasis
- Steps: loss of E-cadherin, degradation of the basement membrane by matrix metalloproteinases, migration, intravasation, survival in the circulation, extravasation and colonisation.
- Carcinomas favour lymphatic spread; sarcomas favour haematogenous spread, most often to the lung. Ovarian carcinoma spreads across the peritoneum (transcoelomic).
- Bone metastases come mainly from breast, prostate, lung, kidney and thyroid.

Grade and stage
Grade describes differentiation (for example the ISUP grade group in prostate cancer). Stage describes extent (TNM) and is usually the stronger prognostic factor.

Paraneoplastic syndromes and markers
- Small cell lung carcinoma: SIADH, ectopic ACTH, Lambert–Eaton syndrome.
- Squamous cell lung carcinoma: hypercalcaemia via PTHrP.
- Renal cell carcinoma: polycythaemia via erythropoietin.
- Tumour markers (PSA, CA-125, CEA, AFP, hCG) mainly monitor disease rather than screen for it.

Applied illustration
A 62-year-old smoker has a hilar mass, hyponatraemia and proximal weakness that improves briefly with repeated effort. This suggests small cell carcinoma with SIADH and Lambert–Eaton syndrome (antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels).

Exam pitfalls
- Grade is not stage.
- Not every '-oma' is benign.
- Carcinoma in situ is not invasive.

Hypersensitivity (Gell and Coombs, 1963)
- Type I (IgE-mediated, immediate): allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells, releasing histamine. Leukotrienes and prostaglandins follow, then a late phase driven by eosinophils and Th2 cytokines (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13). Examples: anaphylaxis, allergic asthma, hay fever.
- Type II (antibody against cell or matrix antigens): damage occurs through complement, phagocytosis or ADCC. Examples: autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, ABO transfusion reactions, haemolytic disease of the newborn, Goodpasture syndrome (anti-type IV collagen).
- Some type II antibodies alter receptor function instead of destroying cells: Graves disease (stimulating anti-TSH-receptor) and myasthenia gravis (anti-acetylcholine receptor).
- Type III (immune complex): complexes deposit in vessels, glomeruli and joints, then activate complement and attract neutrophils. Examples: SLE, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, serum sickness, the Arthus reaction. C3 and C4 are often low.
- Type IV (T-cell-mediated, delayed, peaking at 48–72 hours): Th1 cells activate macrophages, and CD8⁺ T cells kill directly. Examples: the tuberculin test, nickel contact dermatitis, type 1 diabetes, granulomas.

Autoimmunity
Tolerance relies on central deletion in the thymus (AIRE drives expression of tissue antigens) and on peripheral anergy, regulatory T cells (FOXP3) and deletion. Single-gene failures show the importance of each: APECED (AIRE), IPEX (FOXP3) and autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome (Fas).
- Risk factors: HLA type (B27 with ankylosing spondylitis; DR3 and DR4 with type 1 diabetes; DR4 with rheumatoid arthritis), female sex, and infection through molecular mimicry (rheumatic fever).
- Autoantibodies:
- SLE: anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith.
- Rheumatoid arthritis: anti-CCP.
- Systemic sclerosis: anti-centromere (limited), anti-Scl-70 (diffuse).
- Coeliac disease: anti-tTG.
- ANCA vasculitis: PR3-ANCA in granulomatosis with polyangiitis; MPO-ANCA in microscopic polyangiitis.

Immunodeficiency
Suspect immunodeficiency when infections are serious, persistent, unusual or recurrent.
- Antibody defects (bacterial sinopulmonary infections): X-linked agammaglobulinaemia (BTK, absent B cells), common variable immunodeficiency, and selective IgA deficiency, the commonest, which risks anaphylaxis to blood products.
- T-cell and combined defects (viral, fungal and opportunistic infections): DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion, thymic hypoplasia) and severe combined immunodeficiency.
- Phagocyte defects: chronic granulomatous disease, leucocyte adhesion deficiency.
- Complement defects: terminal (C5–C9) deficiency causes recurrent Neisseria infection. C1-inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema, which is bradykinin-mediated and does not respond to antihistamines.
- Secondary causes are far commoner: HIV, immunosuppressive drugs, malnutrition, malignancy, and splenectomy (risk from encapsulated bacteria).

Transplant rejection
- Hyperacute (minutes): pre-formed antibodies.
- Acute (weeks to months): T-cell- or antibody-mediated.
- Chronic (months to years): intimal thickening and fibrosis.
- Graft-versus-host disease follows haematopoietic stem cell transplantation.

Exam pitfalls
- Graves disease and myasthenia gravis are type II.
- Contact dermatitis is type IV.
- A raised mast cell tryptase supports anaphylaxis, but a normal level does not exclude it.

notes.h: Haematology basics: anaemia, haemostasis and haematological malignancy
notes.body:
Anaemia
Anaemia is haemoglobin below the reference range (roughly below 130 g/L in men and 120 g/L in non-pregnant women). Classify it by MCV.
- Microcytic: iron deficiency (low ferritin, raised transferrin or TIBC, low saturation); thalassaemia trait (normal ferritin, MCV low for the Hb, raised HbA₂ in β-trait); anaemia of inflammation; sideroblastic anaemia.
- Normocytic: acute blood loss, chronic disease, chronic kidney disease (low erythropoietin), haemolysis, marrow failure.
- Macrocytic, megaloblastic: B12 or folate deficiency (hypersegmented neutrophils). Pernicious anaemia involves anti-intrinsic factor antibodies.
- Macrocytic, non-megaloblastic: alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, reticulocytosis, myelodysplasia, some drugs.

Haemolysis
- Markers: raised reticulocytes, unconjugated bilirubin and LDH, with low haptoglobin.
- Intrinsic causes: hereditary spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency, pyruvate kinase deficiency, haemoglobinopathies.
- Extrinsic causes: autoimmune (DAT-positive), microangiopathic (schistocytes in TTP and HUS), mechanical valves, malaria.
- Sickle cell disease: deoxygenated HbS polymerises, causing vaso-occlusion, acute chest syndrome, stroke and splenic infarction.
- β-thalassaemia major: excess α-chains precipitate, causing ineffective erythropoiesis, transfusion dependence and iron overload.

Haemostasis
- Primary: von Willebrand factor tethers platelets to collagen via GPIb. Activated platelets release ADP and thromboxane A₂ and aggregate via GPIIb/IIIa and fibrinogen.
- Secondary (cell-based model): tissue factor–VIIa starts thrombin generation. Thrombin activates V, VIII, XI and platelets, and propagation on platelet surfaces produces a thrombin burst, with fibrin cross-linked by XIIIa.
- Controls: antithrombin, proteins C and S, TFPI, plasmin.

Tests
- PT (VII, X, V, II, fibrinogen): reported as the INR for warfarin.
- APTT (XII, XI, IX, VIII plus the common pathway): prolonged in haemophilia and by unfractionated heparin.
- Mucosal bleeding and petechiae suggest a platelet or von Willebrand problem (von Willebrand disease is the commonest inherited bleeding disorder). Haemarthroses suggest haemophilia A (VIII) or B (IX).
- DIC: prolonged PT and APTT, low fibrinogen and platelets, high D-dimer.

Haematological malignancy
- Acute leukaemia: classically at least 20% blasts in blood or marrow (the 2022 WHO and ICC classifications use lower or no blast thresholds for AML with defining genetic changes, such as PML-RARA). Acute promyelocytic leukaemia, t(15;17) PML-RARA, presents with DIC and is treated with all-trans retinoic acid and arsenic trioxide. ALL is the commonest childhood cancer.
- CML: t(9;22) BCR-ABL1, treated with tyrosine kinase inhibitors. CLL: smear cells; the commonest adult leukaemia in the UK.
- JAK2 V617F: polycythaemia vera, and some essential thrombocythaemia and myelofibrosis.
- Lymphoma: Hodgkin (Reed–Sternberg cells, CD15⁺ and CD30⁺); non-Hodgkin, including follicular t(14;18) and Burkitt t(8;14) MYC.
- Myeloma: clonal plasma cells and paraprotein, with CRAB features (hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia, bone lesions).

Applied illustration
A 45-year-old woman with heavy periods has Hb 92 g/L, MCV 71 fL and ferritin 6 µg/L, which indicates iron-deficiency anaemia.

Exam pitfalls
- Ferritin is an acute-phase protein: a normal level does not exclude iron deficiency when inflammation is present.
- Haemophilia prolongs the APTT but not the PT.

Chromosomal disorders
- Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome): about 95% of cases follow meiotic non-disjunction, mostly maternal and age-related. About 4% are Robertsonian translocations, which can be inherited, and a few are mosaic. Features: learning disability, atrioventricular septal defect, duodenal atresia, Hirschsprung disease, hypothyroidism, raised leukaemia risk, and early Alzheimer disease (APP is on chromosome 21).
- Trisomy 18 (Edwards syndrome): overlapping clenched fingers, rocker-bottom feet, cardiac defects, very poor survival.
- Trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome): holoprosencephaly, cleft lip and palate, polydactyly.
- 45,X (Turner syndrome): short stature, ovarian insufficiency, coarctation, bicuspid aortic valve, horseshoe kidney, neonatal lymphoedema.
- 47,XXY (Klinefelter syndrome): tall stature, small firm testes, azoospermia, gynaecomastia, hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.
- 22q11.2 deletion: conotruncal heart defects, thymic hypoplasia, hypocalcaemia, cleft palate, later psychiatric illness.

Single-gene connective tissue disorders
- Marfan syndrome (FBN1, autosomal dominant): aortic root dilatation and dissection, upward lens dislocation, long limbs.
- Osteogenesis imperfecta (mostly COL1A1 or COL1A2): fractures and blue sclerae.

Teratogens
Teratogens act mainly in the embryonic period (weeks 3–8, organogenesis).
- Alcohol: fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, short palpebral fissures, growth restriction, neurodevelopmental problems).
- Sodium valproate: neural tube defects and neurodevelopmental disorders. The MHRA restricts its use through the Pregnancy Prevention Programme and, since January 2024, requires two specialists to agree before it is started in anyone under 55.
- Retinoids such as isotretinoin: craniofacial, cardiac and CNS defects.
- Warfarin: nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses.
- ACE inhibitors (later pregnancy): fetal renal damage and oligohydramnios.
- Infections: rubella (cataracts, deafness, patent ductus arteriosus); cytomegalovirus, the commonest congenital infection (deafness, microcephaly); toxoplasmosis (chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, calcification); syphilis; Zika (microcephaly).
- Poorly controlled maternal diabetes: congenital heart disease, caudal regression, macrosomia.
- Neural tube defects are linked to folate deficiency. Periconceptional folic acid is advised, and in 2021 the UK announced mandatory folic acid fortification of non-wholemeal wheat flour; the 2024 regulations require it by December 2026.

Terminology
- Malformation: an intrinsic error of morphogenesis (ventricular septal defect).
- Deformation: external mechanical force (oligohydramnios causing talipes).
- Disruption: destruction of normal tissue (amniotic bands).
- Sequence: a cascade from one defect. In Potter sequence, renal agenesis causes oligohydramnios, which causes pulmonary hypoplasia, flattened facies and limb deformities.
- Syndrome: several defects with one underlying cause.

Prenatal screening in England
The combined test (nuchal translucency, PAPP-A and hCG) at 11–14 weeks screens for trisomies 21, 18 and 13. A higher-chance result leads to an offer of NIPT (cell-free DNA, still a screening test) or diagnostic CVS or amniocentesis. The anomaly scan at 18+0 to 20+6 weeks follows.

Applied illustration
A newborn with flat facies, upslanting palpebral fissures, a single palmar crease and bilious vomiting suggests trisomy 21 with duodenal atresia ('double bubble' on X-ray).

Exam pitfalls
- NIPT is screening, not diagnosis.
- Translocation Down syndrome is not related to maternal age but carries a recurrence risk.

cards.f: Define metaplasia and give two examples.
cards.b: Reversible replacement of one mature cell type by another, usually as an adaptation to stress. Examples: Barrett oesophagus (squamous to intestinal-type columnar) and bronchial squamous metaplasia in smokers.

cards.f: List the morphological features of reversible cell injury.
cards.b: Cell swelling (hydropic change), fatty change, plasma membrane blebbing, mitochondrial swelling, ER dilatation and ribosome detachment.

cards.f: Name the three nuclear changes of irreversible injury.
cards.b: Pyknosis (shrinkage and condensation), karyorrhexis (fragmentation) and karyolysis (fading as DNA is broken down).

cards.f: Compare necrosis and apoptosis.
cards.b: Necrosis: always pathological, groups of cells, swelling, membrane rupture, inflammation. Apoptosis: energy-dependent, single cells, shrinkage, apoptotic bodies, no inflammation; can be physiological.

cards.f: Which type of necrosis follows cerebral infarction, and why?
cards.b: Liquefactive necrosis. Brain tissue is rich in lipid and poor in supporting stroma, and enzymatic digestion (largely by microglial and recruited enzymes) liquefies it into a cystic cavity.

cards.f: What is caseous necrosis, and where is it typically seen?
cards.b: Necrosis with a soft, cheese-like, structureless appearance inside granulomas. It is typical of tuberculosis.

cards.f: Distinguish dystrophic from metastatic calcification.
cards.b: Dystrophic: in damaged or necrotic tissue with normal serum calcium (atheroma, damaged valves). Metastatic: in normal tissue with hypercalcaemia or hyperphosphataemia (for example in hyperparathyroidism or chronic kidney disease).

cards.f: Why can reperfusion worsen tissue injury?
cards.b: Restored oxygen produces bursts of reactive oxygen species, Ca²⁺ overload follows, and neutrophils and complement are recruited. All of these damage cells that were potentially salvageable.

cards.f: Which serum markers reflect irreversible myocyte injury, and why are they released?
cards.b: Cardiac troponins (I or T), which leak through the damaged sarcolemma. High-sensitivity troponin is the standard test for myocardial infarction.

cards.f: What is fibrinoid necrosis?
cards.b: Damage to vessel walls in which immune complexes and plasma proteins (including fibrin) leak in, giving a bright pink amorphous appearance. Seen in vasculitis and malignant hypertension.

cards.f: What are the cardinal signs of acute inflammation?
cards.b: Rubor (redness), calor (heat), tumor (swelling) and dolor (pain), described by Celsus. Functio laesa (loss of function) was added later.

cards.f: Distinguish an exudate from a transudate.
cards.b: An exudate is protein-rich, with specific gravity above 1.020, and comes from increased vascular permeability in inflammation. A transudate is protein-poor and comes from raised hydrostatic or reduced oncotic pressure.

cards.f: List the steps of leucocyte extravasation and the molecules involved.
cards.b: Rolling (selectins), firm adhesion (integrins LFA-1 and Mac-1 binding ICAM-1), transmigration (PECAM-1), then chemotaxis (C5a, IL-8, LTB₄).

cards.f: Name three cytokines that cause the acute-phase response.
cards.b: IL-1, IL-6 and TNF. They cause fever (via hypothalamic PGE₂), hepatic synthesis of CRP and fibrinogen, and neutrophilia.

cards.f: What is a granuloma?
cards.b: A focus of chronic inflammation made of activated epithelioid macrophages, often with multinucleate giant cells, surrounded by lymphocytes. It is driven by Th1 cells and IFN-γ.

cards.f: Give four causes of non-caseating granulomas.
cards.b: Sarcoidosis, Crohn disease, foreign-body reactions and berylliosis. Others include granulomatosis with polyangiitis and some fungal infections.

cards.f: What defect causes chronic granulomatous disease, and which infections result?
cards.b: Defective NADPH oxidase, so phagocytes lack the respiratory burst. Patients get recurrent infections with catalase-positive organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus.

cards.f: What are the clinical features of leucocyte adhesion deficiency type 1?
cards.b: A CD18 (β₂-integrin) defect impairs firm adhesion. It causes recurrent bacterial infections without pus, marked neutrophilia, and delayed separation of the umbilical cord.

cards.f: Which complement components act as anaphylatoxins, and which as an opsonin?
cards.b: C3a and C5a are anaphylatoxins (mast cell degranulation; C5a is also chemotactic). C3b is the main opsonin.

cards.f: How do M1 and M2 macrophages differ?
cards.b: M1 (classically activated by IFN-γ and microbial products) are microbicidal and pro-inflammatory. M2 (alternatively activated by IL-4 and IL-13) promote tissue repair and fibrosis.

cards.f: Classify tissues by proliferative capacity, with examples.
cards.b: Labile: epidermis, gut epithelium, bone marrow. Stable: hepatocytes, renal tubules, fibroblasts. Permanent: neurones, cardiac myocytes.

cards.f: What is granulation tissue?
cards.b: Pink, granular tissue formed from about day 3 of repair: new capillaries, proliferating fibroblasts and myofibroblasts, and loose matrix with inflammatory cells. It is not a granuloma.

cards.f: Which cytokine is the main driver of fibrosis?
cards.b: TGF-β. It stimulates fibroblast migration and collagen synthesis, and reduces matrix breakdown by inhibiting metalloproteinases.

cards.f: Contrast healing by primary and secondary intention.
cards.b: Primary: clean apposed edges, little granulation tissue, small scar. Secondary: large gaping defect, abundant granulation tissue, marked myofibroblast contraction, larger scar.

cards.f: Why does vitamin C deficiency impair wound healing?
cards.b: Ascorbate is a cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases. Without it, collagen cannot form stable triple helices and cross-links, so it is weak.

cards.f: Distinguish a keloid from a hypertrophic scar.
cards.b: A hypertrophic scar stays within the wound margins and may regress. A keloid grows beyond the margins, is more common in darker skin, and often recurs after excision.

cards.f: How strong is a skin wound at one week and at three months, relative to normal skin?
cards.b: About 10% at one week, when sutures are removed, and about 70–80% by three months. It never fully returns to normal.

cards.f: Which collagen predominates early in a wound, and which replaces it?
cards.b: Type III collagen is laid down early. During remodelling it is replaced by stronger type I collagen.

cards.f: Name the stages of fracture healing.
cards.b: Haematoma and inflammation, soft (fibrocartilaginous) callus, hard (woven bone) callus, then remodelling to lamellar bone.

cards.f: What is the most important local factor delaying wound healing?
cards.b: Infection. It prolongs inflammation and tissue damage. Other local factors include poor perfusion, foreign bodies, mechanical stress and radiation.

cards.f: State Virchow's triad.
cards.b: Endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow (stasis or turbulence) and hypercoagulability of the blood.

cards.f: What is factor V Leiden, and why does it cause thrombosis?
cards.b: A point mutation (R506Q) that makes factor Va resistant to cleavage by activated protein C. It is the commonest inherited thrombophilia in people of European ancestry.

cards.f: How do arterial and venous thrombi differ in composition and prevention?
cards.b: Arterial thrombi are platelet-rich ('white') and prevented with antiplatelet drugs. Venous thrombi are rich in red cells and fibrin ('red') and are prevented or treated with anticoagulants.

cards.f: What are lines of Zahn?
cards.b: Alternating pale layers of platelets and fibrin and dark layers of red cells. They show a thrombus formed in flowing blood, unlike a post-mortem clot.

cards.f: List four possible fates of a thrombus.
cards.b: Resolution by fibrinolysis, propagation, organisation with recanalisation, and embolisation.

cards.f: Where do most pulmonary emboli originate?
cards.b: In deep vein thrombi in the legs, particularly the proximal (popliteal, femoral and iliac) veins.

cards.f: Why are pulmonary infarcts haemorrhagic and relatively uncommon?
cards.b: The lung has a dual blood supply. Bronchial arteries usually keep the tissue alive, so infarction mainly occurs when that supply is also compromised (for example in left heart failure), and blood leaks into the necrotic area.

cards.f: What triad suggests fat embolism syndrome, and when does it occur?
cards.b: Respiratory distress (hypoxaemia), neurological change (confusion) and a petechial rash, typically 24–72 hours after a long-bone or pelvic fracture.

cards.f: Which organs typically develop white (anaemic) infarcts?
cards.b: Solid organs with an end-arterial supply: heart, kidney and spleen.

cards.f: What is paradoxical embolism?
cards.b: A venous embolus that passes into the systemic circulation through a right-to-left shunt, usually a patent foramen ovale, causing for example a stroke.

cards.f: Define a neoplasm.
cards.b: An abnormal mass of tissue whose growth is excessive, uncoordinated with normal tissue, and continues after the stimulus is removed. It is clonal.

cards.f: Distinguish grade from stage.
cards.b: Grade describes how differentiated a tumour looks under the microscope. Stage describes its anatomical extent (TNM). Stage is usually the stronger predictor of prognosis.

cards.f: What is carcinoma in situ?
cards.b: Full-thickness epithelial dysplasia with an intact basement membrane. It has no access to lymphatics or vessels, so it cannot metastasise until it invades.

cards.f: Give three tumours that are malignant despite the '-oma' suffix.
cards.b: Melanoma, mesothelioma and seminoma (lymphoma is another).

cards.f: How do HPV 16 and 18 cause cervical cancer?
cards.b: Viral oncoprotein E6 promotes degradation of p53, and E7 binds and inactivates Rb. Integration of the virus into the host genome increases their expression.

cards.f: Outline the colorectal adenoma–carcinoma sequence.
cards.b: APC loss (Wnt activation) starts the adenoma, KRAS activation drives growth, and TP53 loss accompanies transition to carcinoma (Fearon and Vogelstein, 1990).

cards.f: Which cancers most often metastasise to bone?
cards.b: Breast, prostate, lung, kidney and thyroid. Prostate metastases are typically osteosclerotic; most others are osteolytic.

cards.f: Name three paraneoplastic syndromes of small cell lung cancer.
cards.b: SIADH (hyponatraemia), ectopic ACTH (Cushing syndrome) and Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome.

cards.f: What is a hamartoma?
cards.b: A benign, disorganised overgrowth of tissue native to that site, for example a pulmonary chondroid hamartoma.

cards.f: Why are tumour markers such as CEA used for monitoring rather than screening?
cards.b: They lack sensitivity and specificity for early disease, and benign conditions or smoking can raise them. Serial measurements after treatment are more useful for detecting recurrence.

cards.f: Summarise the four Gell and Coombs hypersensitivity types.
cards.b: I: IgE and mast cells (immediate). II: antibody against cell or matrix antigens. III: immune-complex deposition. IV: T-cell-mediated (delayed).

cards.f: Which hypersensitivity type is Graves disease, and why?
cards.b: Type II. An IgG autoantibody binds and stimulates the TSH receptor, causing hyperthyroidism without cell destruction.

cards.f: Give three examples of type III hypersensitivity.
cards.b: SLE, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and serum sickness. The Arthus reaction is the local form.

cards.f: Why is contact dermatitis a type IV reaction?
cards.b: Haptens such as nickel bind skin proteins. Sensitised T cells react on re-exposure, giving eczema that peaks at 48–72 hours. No antibody is involved.

cards.f: Which autoantibodies are most specific for SLE?
cards.b: Anti-dsDNA (which also tracks disease activity) and anti-Smith. ANA is sensitive but not specific.

cards.f: What does deficiency of the terminal complement components (C5–C9) predispose to?
cards.b: Recurrent, often invasive, Neisseria infections (meningococcal and gonococcal), because the membrane attack complex cannot form.

cards.f: Why can selective IgA deficiency cause transfusion reactions?
cards.b: Some patients make anti-IgA antibodies, which can cause anaphylaxis when they receive blood products containing IgA.

cards.f: What is the defect in X-linked agammaglobulinaemia?
cards.b: Mutation of Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) blocks B-cell maturation. B cells and all immunoglobulin classes are absent, causing bacterial infections after maternal IgG wanes, at around 6 months.

cards.f: Why does hereditary angioedema not respond to antihistamines?
cards.b: C1-inhibitor deficiency causes excess bradykinin, not histamine, so the swelling is bradykinin-mediated.

cards.f: Outline the timing and mechanism of the types of transplant rejection.
cards.b: Hyperacute (minutes): pre-formed antibodies. Acute (weeks to months): T-cell- or antibody-mediated. Chronic (months to years): vascular intimal thickening and fibrosis.

cards.f: How do iron studies distinguish iron deficiency from anaemia of chronic disease?
cards.b: Iron deficiency: low ferritin, high transferrin or TIBC, low saturation. Chronic disease: normal or high ferritin (acute-phase reactant), low or normal TIBC, low serum iron.

cards.f: Give four causes of macrocytic anaemia.
cards.b: B12 deficiency, folate deficiency (both megaloblastic), alcohol, and hypothyroidism. Liver disease, reticulocytosis, myelodysplasia and drugs such as methotrexate are others.

cards.f: Which laboratory findings indicate haemolysis?
cards.b: Raised reticulocytes, unconjugated bilirubin and LDH, with low haptoglobin. The film may show spherocytes or schistocytes.

cards.f: Which clotting test is prolonged in haemophilia A, and which factor is deficient?
cards.b: The APTT. Factor VIII is deficient. The PT is normal.

cards.f: Give the typical coagulation picture in DIC.
cards.b: Prolonged PT and APTT, low fibrinogen, low platelets, raised D-dimer and schistocytes on the film.

cards.f: What genetic lesion defines CML, and how is it treated?
cards.b: t(9;22), the Philadelphia chromosome, which creates the BCR-ABL1 fusion tyrosine kinase. It is treated with tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib.

cards.f: Why is acute promyelocytic leukaemia a medical emergency?
cards.b: It often presents with DIC and life-threatening bleeding. All-trans retinoic acid (with arsenic trioxide) should start as soon as the diagnosis is suspected.

cards.f: Which cells characterise Hodgkin lymphoma, and what is their immunophenotype?
cards.b: Reed–Sternberg cells (large, binucleate, owl-eye nucleoli), typically CD15⁺ and CD30⁺.

cards.f: What are the CRAB features of myeloma?
cards.b: Hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia and bone lesions (lytic).

cards.f: Which mutation underlies most cases of polycythaemia vera?
cards.b: JAK2 V617F, a gain-of-function mutation that activates JAK–STAT signalling independently of erythropoietin.

cards.f: What is the commonest mechanism of trisomy 21?
cards.b: Meiotic non-disjunction, about 95% of cases, mostly in maternal meiosis I, with risk rising with maternal age. Robertsonian translocation (about 4%) and mosaicism make up the rest.

cards.f: Give five features of Down syndrome.
cards.b: Learning disability, atrioventricular septal defect, duodenal atresia, hypothyroidism, raised leukaemia risk, and early Alzheimer disease.

cards.f: What is the karyotype of Turner syndrome, and what are its cardiovascular associations?
cards.b: 45,X (or a mosaic or structural X abnormality). Bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation of the aorta, with a risk of aortic dissection.

cards.f: What are the features of Klinefelter syndrome?
cards.b: 47,XXY: tall stature, small firm testes, azoospermia, gynaecomastia, raised FSH and LH with low testosterone.

cards.f: When is the embryo most vulnerable to teratogens, and why?
cards.b: Weeks 3–8 after conception, during organogenesis. Exposure before then tends to cause either death or full recovery.

cards.f: Distinguish a malformation, a deformation and a disruption.
cards.b: Malformation: intrinsic error of morphogenesis. Deformation: external mechanical force on normal tissue. Disruption: destruction of tissue that was developing normally (for example amniotic bands).

cards.f: Describe the Potter sequence.
cards.b: Renal agenesis (or another cause of severe oligohydramnios) leads to pulmonary hypoplasia, flattened facies and limb deformities. One primary defect sets off a cascade.

cards.f: What are the features of congenital rubella syndrome?
cards.b: Cataracts, sensorineural deafness and congenital heart disease (especially patent ductus arteriosus), often with growth restriction.

cards.f: Which antiepileptic carries the greatest teratogenic risk, and how is it regulated in the UK?
cards.b: Sodium valproate (neural tube defects, neurodevelopmental disorders). The MHRA requires a Pregnancy Prevention Programme for those who could become pregnant, and since January 2024 two specialists must agree before starting it in anyone under 55.

cards.f: Why is NIPT a screening rather than a diagnostic test?
cards.b: Cell-free DNA comes largely from the placenta, so confined placental mosaicism can give false results. A high-chance result needs confirmation by CVS or amniocentesis.

questions.q: Which pattern of necrosis is typically seen in a renal infarct?
questions.why: Ischaemic infarcts of solid organs other than the brain show coagulative necrosis, in which tissue architecture is preserved for some days.

questions.q: Which molecule mediates the firm adhesion of neutrophils to endothelium during extravasation?
questions.why: Selectins mediate rolling. β₂-integrins such as LFA-1, activated by chemokines, bind ICAM-1 for firm adhesion. PECAM-1 mediates transmigration.

questions.q: Which tissue is composed of permanent (non-dividing) cells that heal by scarring?
questions.why: Adult cardiac myocytes have negligible regenerative capacity, so infarcts are replaced by fibrous scar. Hepatocytes and tubular cells are stable; epidermis is labile.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman has a second unprovoked DVT. Testing shows resistance to activated protein C. What is the most likely underlying abnormality?
questions.why: Factor V Leiden (R506Q) makes factor Va resistant to inactivation by activated protein C. It is the commonest inherited thrombophilia in European populations.

questions.q: Which statement about carcinoma in situ of the cervix (CIN 3) is correct?
options: It has invaded the stroma but not lymphatics
It shows full-thickness dysplasia with an intact basement membrane
It is a benign lesion that does not progress
It is staged using the TNM system as T1
questions.why: CIN 3 is full-thickness dysplasia that has not breached the basement membrane, so it cannot metastasise. Without treatment it can progress to invasive carcinoma.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman has ptosis and diplopia that worsen through the day. Antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor are detected. Which hypersensitivity mechanism is this?
questions.why: Myasthenia gravis is type II: autoantibodies bind a fixed cell-surface antigen (the acetylcholine receptor), blocking and down-regulating it and activating complement.

questions.q: A 6-year-old boy has a swollen knee after a minor fall. Platelet count and PT are normal; APTT is prolonged and corrects with mixing with normal plasma. His maternal uncle had similar problems. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Haemarthrosis, an isolated prolonged APTT that corrects on mixing (a factor deficiency, not an inhibitor) and X-linked inheritance indicate haemophilia A (factor VIII). Haemophilia B looks the same and needs factor assays to tell apart.

questions.q: Which congenital infection is the commonest in the UK and a leading non-genetic cause of sensorineural hearing loss?
questions.why: Congenital CMV is the commonest congenital infection and a major cause of sensorineural deafness. Rubella is now rare because of vaccination.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man has Hb 98 g/L, MCV 84 fL, serum iron low, TIBC low and ferritin 420 µg/L. CRP is raised; he has active rheumatoid arthritis. What is the most likely cause of anaemia?
questions.why: Hepcidin, raised by IL-6, traps iron in macrophages: serum iron and TIBC fall, while ferritin, an acute-phase protein, is high. Iron deficiency would give low ferritin and high TIBC.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman collapses and dies suddenly on the tenth day after hip replacement. Which autopsy finding best explains her death?
options: A wedge-shaped haemorrhagic infarct at the right lung base
A saddle embolus at the bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk
A pale wedge-shaped infarct in the spleen
Fat globules in the pulmonary capillaries
questions.why: A large saddle embolus obstructs pulmonary outflow, causing acute right ventricular failure and sudden death. Small emboli cause infarcts but rarely sudden death.

questions.q: Explain the sequence of biochemical events that leads from ischaemia to irreversible cell injury.
markScheme: Loss of oxidative phosphorylation causes ATP depletion; anaerobic glycolysis leads to lactic acidosis and glycogen depletion
Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase fails: Na⁺ and water enter, causing cell and organelle swelling (reversible)
Cytosolic Ca²⁺ rises, activating phospholipases, proteases, endonucleases and mitochondrial permeability transition
Severe membrane damage (lysosomal and plasma membranes) and mitochondrial dysfunction mark irreversibility, with release of enzymes such as troponin
questions.modelAnswer: Without oxygen, oxidative phosphorylation stops and ATP falls. Cells switch to anaerobic glycolysis, using up glycogen and producing lactic acid, and the falling pH clumps nuclear chromatin. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase fails, so Na⁺ and water enter, causing reversible swelling of the cell, ER and mitochondria. Calcium pumps fail, and cytosolic Ca²⁺ activates phospholipases, proteases and endonucleases and opens the mitochondrial permeability transition pore. Once the mitochondria cannot recover and lysosomal and plasma membranes are badly damaged, the injury is irreversible. Enzymes leak out, and contents such as troponin appear in the blood.

questions.q: Compare the causes, cellular composition and outcomes of acute and chronic inflammation.
markScheme: Acute: rapid onset, triggered by infection, trauma or necrosis; neutrophil-rich with oedema
Chronic: persistent infection, prolonged toxic exposure or autoimmunity; lymphocytes, plasma cells and macrophages
Acute outcomes: resolution, abscess, healing by fibrosis or progression to chronic
Chronic inflammation features simultaneous tissue destruction and repair (fibrosis, angiogenesis); may be granulomatous
questions.modelAnswer: Acute inflammation starts within minutes to hours of infection, trauma or necrosis. Vascular changes produce oedema, and neutrophils dominate. It may resolve completely, form an abscess, heal by fibrosis, or become chronic. Chronic inflammation follows persistent infection (tuberculosis), prolonged exposure to irritants (silica) or autoimmunity. Its cells are mainly macrophages, lymphocytes and plasma cells. Tissue destruction, angiogenesis and fibrosis happen together, often causing permanent scarring. A distinctive form is granulomatous inflammation, organised around activated epithelioid macrophages.

questions.q: A 68-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes has a laparotomy wound that breaks down on day 8. List and explain five factors that may have impaired his wound healing.
markScheme: Hyperglycaemia impairs neutrophil function and increases infection risk
Diabetic microvascular and macrovascular disease reduces perfusion and oxygen delivery
Wound infection prolongs inflammation and degrades matrix
Poor nutrition (protein, vitamin C, zinc) limits collagen synthesis
Mechanical stress (coughing, obesity, early lifting) on a wound with only about 10% strength at one week; older age and steroids also relevant
questions.modelAnswer: Several factors probably combined. Hyperglycaemia impairs neutrophil chemotaxis and killing, so wound infection is more likely, and infection is the most important local cause of poor healing because it prolongs inflammation and breaks down matrix. Diabetic vascular disease reduces perfusion, limiting the oxygen fibroblasts need to hydroxylate collagen. Poor nutrition (protein, vitamin C, zinc) restricts collagen synthesis and cross-linking. Older age reduces cell proliferation. Finally, at day 8 the wound has only about 10% of its eventual strength, so strain from coughing, obesity or straining can split it apart (dehiscence).

questions.q: Explain why most infarcts in the heart are pale whereas infarcts in the lung and small intestine are usually haemorrhagic.
markScheme: Heart (and kidney, spleen) are solid organs with end-arterial supply
Occlusion causes coagulative necrosis without blood entering, so pale/white infarct
Lung and intestine have dual or rich collateral supply; blood continues to flow into necrotic loose tissue
Venous occlusion (e.g. volvulus, torsion) and reperfusion also cause red infarcts
questions.modelAnswer: The heart, kidney and spleen are solid organs supplied mainly by end arteries. When one is blocked, the territory it supplies undergoes coagulative necrosis with little blood getting in, so the infarct is pale or white. The lung has both pulmonary and bronchial circulations, and the small bowel has rich arcade collaterals. When infarction does happen there, blood keeps flowing into the dead, loosely structured tissue and the infarct is red. Venous occlusion, as in volvulus or testicular torsion, and reperfusion of a previously pale infarct also produce haemorrhagic infarcts.

questions.q: List four histological features that help distinguish a malignant from a benign tumour, and state the single defining biological feature of malignancy.
markScheme: Nuclear pleomorphism and hyperchromasia
High nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and prominent nucleoli
Increased and atypical mitoses; necrosis; loss of differentiation (anaplasia)
Defining feature: invasion of surrounding tissue (and the capacity to metastasise)
questions.modelAnswer: Malignant tumours often show nuclear pleomorphism with hyperchromatic nuclei, a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and prominent nucleoli. Mitoses are frequent, some with abnormal shapes. There may be central necrosis where growth outruns the blood supply, and loss of normal architecture and differentiation, up to complete anaplasia. Some benign tumours look atypical and some malignant tumours look bland. The defining biological feature of malignancy is invasion beyond the basement membrane into surrounding tissue, which gives access to lymphatics and vessels and so the capacity to metastasise.

questions.q: A 9-month-old boy has had three episodes of pneumonia and otitis media since the age of 6 months. Flow cytometry shows no circulating B cells and serum immunoglobulins of all classes are very low. Explain the most likely diagnosis and why infections began at this age.
markScheme: X-linked agammaglobulinaemia (Bruton), BTK mutation
B-cell maturation arrests at the pre-B-cell stage, so no mature B cells or plasma cells
Maternal IgG transferred across the placenta protects for the first months, waning by about 6 months
Recurrent infections with encapsulated bacteria; treated with immunoglobulin replacement
questions.modelAnswer: This is most likely X-linked agammaglobulinaemia, caused by mutation of Bruton tyrosine kinase. BTK is needed for pre-B-cell receptor signalling, so B-cell development stops at the pre-B stage. Without mature B cells or plasma cells, he makes almost no immunoglobulin of any class. Maternal IgG crossed the placenta in the third trimester and protected him at first. Its half-life is about three weeks, so it had mostly gone by around six months, and recurrent sinopulmonary infections with encapsulated bacteria began. Treatment is lifelong immunoglobulin replacement and prompt antibiotics.

questions.q: Classify anaemia by mean cell volume, giving two causes for each category.
markScheme: Microcytic: iron deficiency, thalassaemia trait (also anaemia of chronic disease, sideroblastic)
Normocytic: acute blood loss, chronic kidney disease, anaemia of chronic disease, haemolysis
Macrocytic megaloblastic: B12 deficiency, folate deficiency
Macrocytic non-megaloblastic: alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, reticulocytosis, myelodysplasia
questions.modelAnswer: Microcytic anaemia (MCV below about 80 fL) is caused mainly by iron deficiency and thalassaemia trait. Anaemia of chronic disease and sideroblastic anaemia are less common causes. Normocytic anaemia includes acute blood loss, anaemia of chronic disease, chronic kidney disease (reduced erythropoietin), haemolysis and marrow infiltration. Macrocytic anaemia (MCV above about 100 fL) is megaloblastic in B12 or folate deficiency, because DNA synthesis is impaired. It is non-megaloblastic with alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, reticulocytosis and myelodysplasia.

questions.q: Explain why the parents of a child with translocation Down syndrome should be offered karyotyping, contrasting this with trisomy 21 due to non-disjunction.
markScheme: Non-disjunction trisomy 21 (about 95%) is sporadic, linked to maternal age, low recurrence risk (about 1% or age-related risk)
Translocation Down syndrome (about 4%) usually involves a Robertsonian translocation, e.g. 14;21
A parent may be a balanced carrier, phenotypically normal
Balanced carrier parents have a substantially raised recurrence risk (higher if mother is carrier; essentially 100% for a 21;21 translocation), so karyotyping guides counselling
questions.modelAnswer: Most Down syndrome (about 95%) results from meiotic non-disjunction, which is sporadic and linked to maternal age. The recurrence risk is low, around 1% or the woman's age-related risk if higher. About 4% of cases have a Robertsonian translocation, for example 14;21, carrying extra chromosome 21 material. In about a quarter to a third of these, one parent is a balanced carrier who is phenotypically normal. Carriers have a substantially raised risk in every pregnancy, higher if the mother carries it. A 21;21 Robertsonian translocation means every viable pregnancy will have Down syndrome. Parental karyotyping therefore identifies carriers and allows accurate counselling, prenatal testing and cascade testing of relatives.

questions.q: Compare the morphology, mechanism and physiological role of apoptosis and necroptosis, and explain why the distinction matters in disease.
markScheme: Apoptosis: cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation, apoptotic bodies, intact membrane, no inflammation
Apoptosis mechanism: caspase-dependent via intrinsic (BCL-2 family, cytochrome c, caspase-9) or extrinsic (death receptor, caspase-8) pathways
Apoptosis roles: development, lymphocyte selection, tissue homeostasis, cytotoxic killing
Necroptosis: necrotic morphology with swelling and membrane rupture, releasing DAMPs and causing inflammation
Necroptosis mechanism: caspase-independent, RIPK1–RIPK3 phosphorylate MLKL, which permeabilises membranes; acts as backup when caspase-8 is inhibited (e.g. by viruses)
Significance: defective apoptosis contributes to cancer and autoimmunity; necroptosis contributes to inflammatory injury (e.g. ischaemia–reperfusion) and is a potential drug target
questions.modelAnswer:
Apoptosis is a caspase-dependent programme. The cell shrinks, chromatin condenses and apoptotic bodies are cleared without inflammation. Intrinsic (BCL-2 family, cytochrome c, caspase-9) and extrinsic (death receptor, caspase-8) pathways converge on caspases 3 and 7. Apoptosis shapes development, deletes autoreactive lymphocytes and mediates cytotoxic T-cell killing.

Necroptosis looks like necrosis: the cell swells and its membrane ruptures, releasing damage-associated molecules that provoke inflammation. It is caspase-independent: RIPK1 and RIPK3 phosphorylate MLKL, which disrupts the membrane, providing a back-up when viruses block caspase-8.

The distinction matters in disease. Too little apoptosis contributes to cancer (BCL-2 overexpression) and autoimmunity (Fas defects). Necroptosis amplifies inflammatory tissue damage, for example in ischaemia–reperfusion injury, which makes its pathway a possible target for treatment.

questions.q: A 24-year-old woman is admitted with anaphylaxis after eating peanuts. Explain the immunological sequence from initial sensitisation to the acute reaction, including the biphasic response and the value of mast cell tryptase measurement.
markScheme: Sensitisation: allergen presented to naive CD4⁺ T cells, which differentiate to Th2 (IL-4, IL-13) driving B-cell class switching to IgE
IgE binds FcεRI on mast cells and basophils
Re-exposure: allergen cross-links bound IgE, causing degranulation (histamine, tryptase) with vasodilatation, increased permeability, bronchospasm
Newly synthesised leukotrienes and prostaglandins and later cytokines (IL-5 recruiting eosinophils) underlie the late phase; biphasic reactions can recur hours later
Tryptase peaks about 1–2 hours after onset; serial samples (with a baseline) support mast cell activation, but a normal level does not exclude anaphylaxis
questions.modelAnswer: At first exposure, dendritic cells present peanut antigens to naive CD4⁺ T cells, which become Th2 cells. Their IL-4 and IL-13 drive B cells to switch to IgE. The IgE binds high-affinity FcεRI receptors on mast cells and basophils. On re-exposure, the allergen cross-links bound IgE and the cells degranulate within minutes, releasing histamine and tryptase. This causes vasodilatation, leaky vessels and bronchospasm. The cells then make leukotrienes and prostaglandins, followed by cytokines such as IL-5 that recruit eosinophils. This late phase explains why symptoms can recur hours later in a biphasic reaction. Tryptase peaks one to two hours after onset. Timed samples compared with a baseline support the diagnosis, but a normal result does not exclude anaphylaxis.

questions.q: Mr Okafor, a 58-year-old smoker, has central chest pain for 90 minutes. ECG shows ST elevation in the anterior leads and high-sensitivity troponin is markedly raised. He undergoes primary percutaneous coronary intervention but dies of a ventricular arrhythmia on day 4. Describe the cellular events of myocardial ischaemic injury from the first minutes, explain the effect of reperfusion, and describe the macroscopic and microscopic appearance of the infarct you would expect at autopsy on day 4.
markScheme: Within seconds: aerobic metabolism stops, ATP falls, contractility lost
Reversible injury for roughly 20–30 minutes: swelling, glycogen loss, lactic acidosis
Irreversible injury: membrane damage, Ca²⁺ overload, mitochondrial dysfunction; troponin release
Necrosis progresses as a wavefront from subendocardium to epicardium over hours
Reperfusion salvages myocardium still reversibly injured, limiting infarct size
Reperfusion injury: ROS, Ca²⁺ overload, neutrophil infiltration, contraction band necrosis, microvascular obstruction
Day 4 macroscopic: soft yellow-tan centre with hyperaemic border
Day 4 microscopic: coagulative necrosis with loss of nuclei and striations; dense neutrophil infiltrate beginning to break down; early macrophages at margins
Ventricular arrhythmias common early due to electrical instability of ischaemic border zone
Notes timeline thereafter: macrophages, granulation tissue (1–2 weeks), scar by about 6–8 weeks; risk of rupture around days 3–7
questions.modelAnswer:
Within seconds of coronary occlusion, myocytes switch to anaerobic glycolysis and contraction fails. ATP falls, lactate builds up and pH drops. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase fails, so cells swell and lose glycogen. For roughly the first 20–30 minutes of severe ischaemia these changes are reversible. After that, mitochondrial damage, Ca²⁺ overload and membrane disruption make the injury irreversible, and troponin leaks into the blood. Necrosis spreads as a wavefront from the subendocardium, the most vulnerable zone, towards the epicardium over several hours. This is why time to reperfusion largely decides infarct size.

Primary PCI restores flow and saves myocytes that are still reversibly injured. Reperfusion has its own costs. Oxygen returning produces a burst of reactive oxygen species, Ca²⁺ floods in and causes hypercontraction (contraction band necrosis), and neutrophils plug capillaries (microvascular obstruction). Reperfused infarcts are often haemorrhagic. The ischaemic border zone remains electrically unstable, which explains ventricular arrhythmias in the first days.

At day 4, the infarct would be visible as a soft, yellow-tan area with a red, hyperaemic border, typically in the anterior left ventricle and septum (left anterior descending territory). Microscopy would show coagulative necrosis: myocytes with intensely eosinophilic cytoplasm, loss of nuclei and striations, and preserved outlines. There would be a heavy neutrophil infiltrate, peaking at about days 1–3 and now breaking down, with macrophages starting to arrive at the margins to clear debris. Granulation tissue would appear at the edges over the next one to two weeks, and the area would be replaced by collagen scar by about 6–8 weeks. Between days 3 and 7 the softened wall is at its weakest, which is the period of greatest risk of free wall, septal or papillary muscle rupture.

questions.q: Mrs Begum, a 45-year-old woman who moved to the UK from Bangladesh, has had cough, night sweats and weight loss for three months. Chest X-ray shows a cavitating right upper lobe lesion. Sputum is positive for acid-fast bacilli. Explain the immunopathological basis of the granulomatous inflammation in tuberculosis, why caseation and cavitation occur, and how this immunology relates to latent infection and reactivation.
markScheme: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is inhaled and phagocytosed by alveolar macrophages; survives by blocking phagolysosome fusion
Dendritic cells present antigen; CD4⁺ Th1 response develops over 2–6 weeks with IL-12 from macrophages
IFN-γ from Th1 cells activates macrophages (M1), enhancing killing (nitric oxide, ROS)
Activated macrophages become epithelioid cells and fuse into Langhans giant cells; TNF essential for granuloma formation and maintenance
Granuloma walls off bacilli; caseous necrosis in centre from macrophage death and hypoxia
Type IV hypersensitivity component (tuberculin reaction)
Liquefaction of caseum and erosion into a bronchus produces cavitation, high bacillary load and infectiousness
Primary infection (Ghon focus and complex) usually contained: latent infection
Reactivation when cell-mediated immunity falls: HIV, anti-TNF therapy, diabetes, malnutrition, older age, immunosuppression
Secondary TB favours apices (high oxygen tension)
Clinical relevance: screening for latent TB before anti-TNF; interferon-gamma release assays
Systemic features from TNF and IL-1 (fever, weight loss)
questions.modelAnswer:
Inhaled Mycobacterium tuberculosis is engulfed by alveolar macrophages. It survives inside them by blocking acidification of the phagosome and its fusion with lysosomes, and multiplies for several weeks. Dendritic cells carry antigen to the hilar lymph nodes, where IL-12 drives naive CD4⁺ T cells to become Th1 cells. About three to six weeks after infection, these Th1 cells return and release IFN-γ. This activates macrophages, which produce nitric oxide and reactive oxygen species and become better at killing.

The granuloma organises this response. Activated macrophages turn into epithelioid cells and some fuse into multinucleate Langhans giant cells, surrounded by a cuff of lymphocytes and later fibroblasts. TNF from macrophages and T cells is needed to form and maintain granulomas. The same cell-mediated response produces the type IV hypersensitivity seen in the tuberculin skin test.

In the centre of the granuloma, macrophages die from bacterial toxicity, hypoxia and immune attack, leaving caseous necrosis: amorphous, cheese-like debris. If the caseous material liquefies and erodes into a bronchus, it drains and leaves a cavity. Oxygen-rich cavity walls support huge numbers of bacilli, which explains Mrs Begum's smear-positive sputum and her infectiousness. Reactivation disease favours the well-oxygenated apices.

In most people, primary infection (the Ghon focus and enlarged hilar nodes forming the Ghon complex) is contained by granulomas and heals by fibrosis and calcification. Viable bacilli can persist, however: this is latent infection. Reactivation occurs when cell-mediated immunity weakens through HIV infection, anti-TNF therapy, corticosteroids, diabetes, malnutrition, renal failure or age. This is why latent TB is screened for, often with interferon-gamma release assays, before biological therapy. Her systemic symptoms reflect circulating TNF and IL-1, which cause fever, night sweats and cachexia.

questions.q: Dev, a 22-year-old man, sustains a 4 cm clean laceration to his forearm, which is sutured in the emergency department. His friend Leo sustains a large, contaminated abrasion of the thigh in the same motorcycle accident, which is cleaned and left open to heal. Compare the sequence of events by which each wound heals, explaining the cellular and molecular basis, and identify the complications each is most at risk of.
markScheme: Dev: primary intention; Leo: secondary intention
Both: haemostasis with fibrin clot; acute inflammation with neutrophils (24–48 h), then macrophages (by day 3) clearing debris and releasing growth factors
Proliferation: granulation tissue (fibroblasts, VEGF-driven angiogenesis); much more abundant in secondary intention
Epithelialisation: rapid across narrow incision (24–48 h); slow from margins in large defect
Collagen: type III early, replaced by type I during remodelling; TGF-β key fibrogenic signal
Wound contraction by myofibroblasts prominent in secondary intention, reducing defect size
Strength: about 10% at one week, 70–80% by three months
Dev risks: infection, dehiscence, hypertrophic scar or keloid, suture marks
Leo risks: infection (contamination), larger scar, contracture, hypertrophic scarring, delayed healing
Factors such as nutrition, blood supply and foreign material influence both
questions.modelAnswer:
Dev's sutured laceration heals by primary intention. Leo's open, contaminated abrasion heals by secondary intention. The processes are the same, but they differ in scale.

In both wounds, haemostasis comes first: platelets aggregate and a fibrin clot forms, which plugs the defect and provides a scaffold. Within 24 hours, neutrophils migrate in to remove bacteria and debris. By about day 3, macrophages take over. They clear dead tissue and release growth factors (PDGF, FGF, TGF-β, VEGF) that drive the next phase.

In the proliferative phase, fibroblasts migrate in and make extracellular matrix, and VEGF-driven angiogenesis produces granulation tissue. In Dev's wound, the gap is narrow, so only a little granulation tissue is needed. The epidermis bridges the incision within one to two days, and collagen spans the wound by the end of the first week. Leo's wound must fill a large defect from the base up, so granulation tissue is abundant. Epithelial cells migrate slowly in from the edges, and his wound also has to deal with heavy bacterial contamination, which prolongs inflammation. Myofibroblasts, which contain smooth-muscle actin, contract his wound markedly and reduce its area.

Remodelling continues for months in both wounds. Type III collagen is replaced by type I, TGF-β drives synthesis, and metalloproteinases reshape the matrix. Tensile strength is only about 10% of normal at one week and reaches about 70–80% at three months. It never fully recovers.

Dev's main risks are wound infection, dehiscence if the wound is strained early, and hypertrophic or keloid scarring. Leo's risks are greater. Contamination makes infection likely and delays healing. He will have a larger scar, and strong contraction over the thigh can produce a contracture or hypertrophic scar. Debriding foreign material and providing good nutrition and perfusion will help healing in both.

questions.q: Mrs Thompson, a 67-year-old woman, is admitted with a fractured neck of femur and undergoes hemiarthroplasty. She has metastatic breast cancer and remains largely immobile. On day 6 she develops a swollen, tender left calf, and on day 9 sudden pleuritic chest pain, breathlessness and haemoptysis. Using Virchow's triad, explain why she developed venous thrombosis, describe the possible fates of the thrombus, and explain the pathophysiology of her presentation on day 9.
markScheme: Virchow stasis: immobility, post-operative bed rest
Endothelial injury: surgical trauma near hip, vessel manipulation
Hypercoagulability: malignancy (tissue factor expression, procoagulants), surgery (acute-phase response), age
DVT originates in calf veins, especially valve pockets, and may propagate proximally
Fates: resolution by fibrinolysis, organisation and recanalisation, propagation, embolism
Venous thrombus composition: red cells and fibrin; lines of Zahn
Embolus travels via IVC and right heart to pulmonary arteries
Pleuritic pain and haemoptysis suggest peripheral (smaller) embolus causing pulmonary infarction (haemorrhagic due to dual supply, more likely when bronchial supply compromised)
Breathlessness from ventilation–perfusion mismatch, hypoxaemia; large emboli cause right ventricular strain or death
Management principles: anticoagulation (LMWH or DOAC, considering cancer), thromboprophylaxis should have been given; assessment as per NICE NG158
Long-term complications: post-thrombotic syndrome, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension
questions.modelAnswer:
All three elements of Virchow's triad are present.
- Stasis: she has been largely immobile since the fracture and operation, so blood pools in the calf veins, particularly in the valve pockets, where local hypoxia activates the endothelium.
- Endothelial injury: the fracture and the operation near the hip damaged and manipulated the femoral vessels.
- Hypercoagulability: metastatic cancer is strongly prothrombotic, because tumour cells express tissue factor and other procoagulants. Major surgery adds an acute-phase rise in fibrinogen and factor VIII, and her age adds further risk.
Together these explain a deep vein thrombosis in the calf by day 6, despite the routine use of thromboprophylaxis in such patients.

Venous thrombi form in slow flow and consist mainly of red cells trapped in fibrin, with platelet layers forming lines of Zahn. Once formed, a thrombus may be lysed by fibrinolysis, propagate up into the popliteal and femoral veins, or organise. Organisation involves ingrowth of granulation tissue and recanalisation, which often destroys the valves and leads to post-thrombotic syndrome. Or it may fragment and embolise. Proximal thrombi carry the greatest risk of embolism.

On day 9, a fragment travelled through the inferior vena cava and right heart into the pulmonary arteries. Pleuritic pain and haemoptysis suggest a smaller, peripheral embolus that has caused pulmonary infarction. Infarction is uncommon because the bronchial circulation usually keeps lung tissue alive. It is more likely when perfusion is poor, and the infarcts are haemorrhagic and wedge-shaped, with their base on the pleura, which explains the pleuritic pain. Breathlessness and hypoxaemia result from ventilation–perfusion mismatch. A larger embolus could have caused acute right ventricular failure and collapse.

She would be assessed using the NICE NG158 pathway (Wells score, imaging such as CT pulmonary angiography) and anticoagulated, with the drug chosen to suit her cancer and bleeding risk. Later complications include post-thrombotic syndrome and chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension.

questions.q: 'Virchow's triad, described in the nineteenth century, remains a sufficient framework for understanding thrombosis in modern clinical practice.' Discuss.
markScheme: Explains the triad: endothelial injury, abnormal flow, hypercoagulability; historical attribution (later synthesis of Virchow's work)
Arterial thrombosis: plaque rupture and erosion fit endothelial injury; turbulence; platelet-rich; antiplatelet therapy
Venous thrombosis: stasis and hypercoagulability dominate; valve-pocket hypoxia
Inherited thrombophilias (factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, protein C/S, antithrombin deficiency) fit the hypercoagulability limb
Acquired states: cancer, pregnancy, oestrogen, antiphospholipid syndrome, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, nephrotic syndrome
Modern refinements: endothelium as active regulator (thrombomodulin, NO, prostacyclin, TFPI) rather than passive lining
Immunothrombosis: neutrophil extracellular traps, monocyte tissue factor, complement; COVID-19-associated thrombosis
Cell-based model of coagulation replaces cascade; platelets and microparticles
Vaccine-induced immune thrombocytopenia and thrombosis (2021) and HIT: antibody-mediated platelet activation, a mechanism not anticipated by the triad
Practical value: risk assessment for thromboprophylaxis (e.g. hospital VTE risk assessment), multiple simultaneous factors
Limits: triad describes categories not mechanisms; interaction between limbs; poor at predicting individual risk
Balanced conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Virchow's triad of endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow and hypercoagulability is still taught as the foundation of thrombosis. The modern triad is a later synthesis attributed to Virchow, not a list he himself set out, but it remains strikingly useful.

It explains the difference between arterial and venous disease. In arteries, plaque rupture or erosion exposes collagen and tissue factor, and platelets aggregate under high shear, forming white thrombi that are prevented with antiplatelet drugs. In veins, stasis in valve pockets combined with hypercoagulability produces red, fibrin-rich thrombi treated with anticoagulants. The hypercoagulability limb accommodates inherited thrombophilias (factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, deficiencies of protein C, protein S and antithrombin) and acquired states such as cancer, pregnancy, oestrogen therapy and antiphospholipid syndrome. In practice, hospital VTE risk assessment follows its logic: immobility, surgical trauma and procoagulant states are added up to decide on thromboprophylaxis.

Yet as a sufficient framework it falls short. The triad treats its limbs as separate categories, whereas we now know the endothelium is an active regulator. It expresses thrombomodulin, TFPI, prostacyclin and nitric oxide, and inflammation switches it to a prothrombotic state without visible injury. The cell-based model of coagulation puts platelet surfaces, not a linear cascade, at the centre of thrombin generation.

Immunothrombosis is the clearest gap. Neutrophil extracellular traps, monocyte tissue factor and complement activation link infection and inflammation to clotting, and they were prominent in COVID-19-associated thrombosis. Antibody-mediated syndromes show further mechanisms that the triad does not explain. In heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and in vaccine-induced immune thrombocytopenia and thrombosis (recognised in 2021), antibodies against platelet factor 4 activate platelets directly, causing thrombosis despite a low platelet count.

The triad also predicts individual risk poorly. Most people with one risk factor never develop thrombosis, and the limbs interact, as when cancer contributes to all three.

In conclusion, the triad remains a valuable organising heuristic and guide to prevention, but it is not sufficient. A modern account adds active endothelial biology, cell-based coagulation and immune mechanisms. Its lasting value lies in prompting clinicians to look for several interacting causes.

questions.q: Mr Harris, a 64-year-old man, presents with iron-deficiency anaemia and a change in bowel habit. Colonoscopy shows an ulcerated tumour in the sigmoid colon and two small tubular adenomas elsewhere. Biopsy confirms adenocarcinoma. CT shows two liver lesions. Explain the stepwise molecular pathogenesis of his tumour, the mechanisms by which it invaded and metastasised, and how grade and stage contribute to his prognosis and management.
markScheme: Adenoma–carcinoma sequence (Fearon and Vogelstein): APC loss activates Wnt/β-catenin, forming adenoma
KRAS activation drives growth (larger adenoma); loss of SMAD4/18q
TP53 loss accompanies transition to invasive carcinoma
Chromosomal instability pathway in most; alternative MSI pathway (mismatch repair deficiency) and serrated pathway (BRAF, CpG methylation)
Accumulation of mutations more important than order; adenomas show field risk
Invasion: loss of E-cadherin, epithelial–mesenchymal transition, matrix metalloproteinases breach basement membrane and muscularis mucosae
Metastasis: intravasation, portal venous drainage, liver is first capillary bed; colonisation requires favourable microenvironment ('seed and soil')
Iron deficiency from chronic occult bleeding from ulcerated tumour
Grade: differentiation; stage: TNM; liver metastases mean M1, stage IV
