Prognosis driven mainly by stage; liver-limited disease may be resectable with curative intent with systemic therapy
Molecular testing: MMR/MSI (Lynch screening, immunotherapy), RAS and BRAF status guide anti-EGFR therapy
MDT management
questions.modelAnswer:
Most colorectal cancers develop through the adenoma–carcinoma sequence described by Fearon and Vogelstein. The first step is usually loss of APC, either inherited, as in familial adenomatous polyposis, or acquired. Without APC, β-catenin is not degraded and Wnt target genes drive proliferation in the crypts, forming an adenoma. Activating KRAS mutations then promote growth of the adenoma. Loss of SMAD4 and other genes on 18q, and finally inactivation of TP53, accompany the change to invasive carcinoma. The accumulation of these changes matters more than their exact order. Most tumours follow this chromosomal instability pathway. Others arise through mismatch repair deficiency (microsatellite instability) or the serrated pathway (BRAF mutation, CpG island methylation). Mr Harris's additional adenomas show that his whole colon is at risk.

Invasion requires the cells to loosen their adhesions. Loss of E-cadherin and partial epithelial–mesenchymal transition make the cells motile, and matrix metalloproteinases break down the basement membrane. Once the tumour crosses the muscularis mucosae into the submucosa, it is invasive and can reach lymphatics and veins. The colon drains through the portal vein, so the liver is the first capillary bed that circulating tumour cells meet. Only a small fraction survive in the circulation, leave the vessels and grow. The 'seed and soil' idea explains why the liver microenvironment suits them. His iron deficiency reflects chronic occult bleeding from the ulcerated tumour surface.

Grade describes differentiation, and poorly differentiated tumours behave more aggressively. Stage is the dominant prognostic factor. With liver metastases he has M1, stage IV disease. Even so, a multidisciplinary team may consider liver-limited metastases resectable with curative intent, combined with systemic therapy. Molecular testing guides treatment. MMR or MSI status, which NICE recommends for all colorectal cancers, identifies possible Lynch syndrome and suitability for immunotherapy. RAS and BRAF status determine whether anti-EGFR antibodies are likely to work.

questions.q: 'Cancer is a genetic disease, but it cannot be understood by studying the cancer cell alone.' Discuss, with reference to the tumour microenvironment, carcinogens and the host immune response.
markScheme: Genetic basis: oncogenes, tumour suppressors, caretaker genes; clonal evolution; inherited predisposition (BRCA, Lynch, APC)
Carcinogens act via DNA damage: tobacco, UV, aflatoxin; mutational signatures
Non-genotoxic and infectious drivers: chronic inflammation (H. pylori, hepatitis, ulcerative colitis), HPV oncoproteins, hormones
Tumour microenvironment: cancer-associated fibroblasts, extracellular matrix, hypoxia
Angiogenesis: VEGF and the angiogenic switch; anti-VEGF therapy
Inflammation as hallmark: tumour-associated macrophages promote growth and invasion
Immune surveillance and immunoediting (elimination, equilibrium, escape); higher cancer incidence in immunosuppression (transplant recipients, HIV)
Immune evasion via PD-L1, loss of MHC class I; checkpoint inhibitors succeed by acting on host T cells
Metastasis depends on host niches ('seed and soil', Paget 1889)
Epigenetic and non-genetic heterogeneity, drug-tolerant states
Normal tissues carry many driver mutations without cancer (clonal haematopoiesis, normal oesophagus) showing context matters
Conclusion: genetic changes are necessary but host and environmental context determine outcome
questions.modelAnswer:
There are good reasons to call cancer a genetic disease. Tumours arise by clonal expansion of cells carrying mutations that activate oncogenes (KRAS, MYC), inactivate tumour suppressors (TP53, RB1) or disable caretaker genes (mismatch repair, BRCA). Inherited variants in these genes cause cancer syndromes. Many carcinogens act through DNA damage: tobacco hydrocarbons, UV light and aflatoxin each leave characteristic mutational signatures.

Yet the genotype alone does not determine whether a cancer appears or how it behaves. Sequencing of normal tissues has shown that ageing oesophagus, skin and blood carry many clones with driver mutations that never become cancer (for example clonal haematopoiesis). Context decides the outcome. Chronic inflammation promotes tumours without being strongly mutagenic: Helicobacter pylori gastritis, chronic hepatitis and ulcerative colitis all raise cancer risk through cytokines, cell turnover and oxidative stress. Hormones drive breast and prostate cancer.

The tumour microenvironment is an active partner. Cancer-associated fibroblasts remodel the matrix and secrete growth factors. Hypoxia selects aggressive clones and triggers the angiogenic switch through VEGF. Tumour-associated macrophages can encourage invasion and suppress immunity. Paget's 'seed and soil' hypothesis (1889) recognised that metastasis depends on whether distant organs are hospitable to tumour cells.

The host immune response is decisive. Immunoediting describes elimination, equilibrium and escape. Transplant recipients and people with HIV have higher rates of virus-associated and other cancers, showing that immunity normally holds tumours back. Tumours escape by losing MHC class I or expressing PD-L1. Checkpoint inhibitors produce lasting responses by acting on the host's T cells, not on the cancer cell, and they work best in tumours with many mutations, such as MSI-high cancers and melanoma. Genetics and immunity are linked here: more mutations mean more neoantigens.

Non-genetic heterogeneity also matters. Epigenetic states and drug-tolerant persister cells contribute to treatment failure.

In conclusion, mutations are necessary for cancer but not sufficient. Cancer is better seen as an evolving ecosystem in which genetically altered cells interact with stroma, blood vessels, immune cells and the wider host environment. Some of the most successful modern treatments target this ecosystem rather than the mutant cell itself.

questions.q: Chloe, a 26-year-old woman, presents with a photosensitive malar rash, painful swollen small joints of the hands, mouth ulcers and ankle oedema. Investigations: positive ANA, high anti-dsDNA, low C3 and C4, lymphopenia, and urine dipstick with 3+ protein and blood. Explain the immunopathogenesis of her condition, relating each investigation finding to the mechanism, and discuss the basis of tissue damage in her kidneys.
markScheme: Diagnosis: systemic lupus erythematosus with likely lupus nephritis
Loss of tolerance: genetic (HLA, complement C1q/C4 deficiency), hormonal (female predominance), environmental (UV light, drugs, EBV)
Defective clearance of apoptotic cells exposes nuclear antigens; UV-induced keratinocyte apoptosis
Plasmacytoid dendritic cells produce type I interferon (interferon signature); autoreactive B cells and T-cell help
Autoantibodies to nuclear antigens: ANA (sensitive), anti-dsDNA (specific, tracks activity), anti-Smith
Type III hypersensitivity: immune complexes deposit in glomeruli, skin, joints, serosa
Complement activation consumes C3 and C4 (low levels), recruits neutrophils, causes inflammation
Lymphopenia from antibody-mediated destruction and interferon effects; type II mechanisms also cause haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia
Lupus nephritis: subendothelial and mesangial deposits; proliferative glomerulonephritis causing haematuria, proteinuria, oedema
Renal biopsy for classification (ISN/RPS classes I–VI); guides immunosuppression
Treatment principles: hydroxychloroquine for all, immunosuppression for nephritis (e.g. mycophenolate), steroids; biologics (belimumab, anifrolumab)
Monitor anti-dsDNA and complement for activity
questions.modelAnswer:
Chloe has systemic lupus erythematosus, with features suggesting lupus nephritis. SLE results from loss of tolerance to nuclear self-antigens in a genetically susceptible person. Contributing factors include HLA type, rare deficiencies of early complement components (C1q, C4), female sex and environmental triggers. UV light makes keratinocytes undergo apoptosis, exposing nuclear antigens, which explains her photosensitive rash. Apoptotic debris is cleared poorly, so nucleic acid antigens stimulate plasmacytoid dendritic cells to produce type I interferon. This activates autoreactive B cells, which with T-cell help make high-affinity IgG autoantibodies.

Each investigation reflects this process:
- ANA is very sensitive for SLE but not specific.
- Anti-dsDNA is highly specific, and its titre tends to rise with disease activity, especially nephritis.
- Low C3 and C4: immune complexes activate the classical complement pathway, consuming both components. Low complement also signals active disease.
- Lymphopenia: antibody-mediated destruction and interferon effects. Similar type II mechanisms can cause haemolytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia.

Most of the tissue damage is type III hypersensitivity. Circulating or locally formed DNA–anti-DNA complexes deposit in glomeruli, synovium, skin and serosal surfaces. There they activate complement, generating C5a, which recruits neutrophils and monocytes and causes inflammation. In the kidney, mesangial deposits cause mild disease. Subendothelial deposits lie in contact with blood, so they cause proliferative glomerulonephritis, with endothelial damage, haematuria and proteinuria. Heavy proteinuria lowers plasma oncotic pressure, which explains her ankle oedema.

A renal biopsy is needed to classify the nephritis (ISN/RPS classes I–VI) and to decide treatment. Hydroxychloroquine is recommended for all patients. Active proliferative nephritis needs immunosuppression, such as mycophenolate with corticosteroids, and biologics such as belimumab (anti-BLyS) and anifrolumab (anti-type I interferon receptor) are now options for selected patients. Anti-dsDNA, complement levels and urine protein are used to monitor activity.

questions.q: Grace, a 19-year-old student of West African heritage with known sickle cell disease (HbSS), presents with severe pain in her back and legs after an exam period, with fever and dehydration. Hb is 68 g/L (her baseline is about 80 g/L), reticulocytes are raised, and bilirubin is raised. Explain the molecular and cellular basis of sickle cell disease, why crises are precipitated, and the mechanisms of its acute and chronic complications.
markScheme: Autosomal recessive; point mutation in β-globin gene codon 6 (Glu to Val), HbS
Deoxygenated HbS polymerises into long fibres, distorting red cells into sickle shapes
Initially reversible; repeated sickling damages membrane causing irreversibly sickled, dehydrated, rigid cells
Vaso-occlusion: rigid cells plus adhesion to endothelium, leucocytes, inflammation obstruct microvessels causing ischaemia and pain
Precipitants: hypoxia, dehydration (raises HbS concentration), acidosis, infection, cold, stress
Haemolysis: chronic extravascular and intravascular, causing anaemia, reticulocytosis, unconjugated bilirubin, gallstones; free Hb scavenges NO
Acute complications: vaso-occlusive crisis, acute chest syndrome, stroke, splenic sequestration, aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19), priapism
Chronic: autosplenectomy with encapsulated organism infection risk, avascular necrosis, nephropathy, retinopathy, pulmonary hypertension, leg ulcers
HbF protects by inhibiting polymerisation; basis of hydroxycarbamide
Management principles: analgesia, hydration, oxygen if hypoxic, treat infection; prophylactic penicillin and vaccines; transfusion for selected complications
questions.modelAnswer:
Sickle cell disease is autosomal recessive. A point mutation in codon 6 of the β-globin gene replaces glutamate with valine, producing HbS. When deoxygenated, HbS exposes a hydrophobic patch that lets molecules bind to each other and polymerise into long, rigid fibres. These distort the red cell into a sickle shape. Sickling is at first reversible on reoxygenation, but repeated cycles damage the membrane, dehydrate the cell and leave irreversibly sickled cells.

Vaso-occlusion results from both rigid cells and adhesion. Sickled cells, reticulocytes and activated leucocytes stick to inflamed endothelium and block small vessels, causing ischaemia, infarction and severe pain. Polymerisation depends strongly on HbS concentration and deoxygenation. Dehydration concentrates HbS, hypoxia and acidosis increase deoxygenation (acidosis shifts the dissociation curve right), and infection adds fever and inflammation. Stress and cold also contribute. Grace's exam stress, fever and dehydration all fit.

Sickled cells are fragile, so haemolysis is continuous, mostly extravascular. This explains her chronic anaemia, raised reticulocytes and unconjugated bilirubin, and the frequent pigment gallstones. Free haemoglobin from intravascular haemolysis scavenges nitric oxide, contributing to vasculopathy and pulmonary hypertension.

Acute complications include:
- Painful vaso-occlusive crises.
- Acute chest syndrome (new infiltrate with chest symptoms), a leading cause of death.
- Stroke.
- Splenic sequestration in children.
- Aplastic crisis when parvovirus B19 halts red cell production (reticulocytes fall).
- Priapism.
Chronic damage includes autosplenectomy from repeated splenic infarction, which carries a lifelong risk from encapsulated bacteria and requires penicillin prophylaxis and vaccination. Avascular necrosis of the femoral head, nephropathy, proliferative retinopathy and leg ulcers also occur.

Fetal haemoglobin inhibits polymerisation, which is why hydroxycarbamide, which raises HbF, reduces crises. Her acute management involves prompt analgesia, hydration, oxygen if she is hypoxic, looking for and treating infection, and close monitoring for acute chest syndrome.

questions.q: Mr Novak, a 38-year-old man, presents with gum bleeding, widespread bruising and fatigue. Bloods: Hb 85 g/L, white cell count 2.1 × 10⁹/L, platelets 18 × 10⁹/L, PT and APTT prolonged, fibrinogen very low, D-dimer markedly raised. The blood film shows abnormal promyelocytes with multiple Auer rods. Explain the most likely diagnosis, the molecular basis of the disease and its treatment, and the pathophysiology of the coagulation abnormality.
markScheme: Acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL), a subtype of AML
Cytopenias from marrow replacement by leukaemic promyelocytes (anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia)
t(15;17) creates PML-RARA fusion gene
PML-RARA acts as a transcriptional repressor of retinoic acid target genes, blocking differentiation at promyelocyte stage; disrupts PML nuclear bodies
All-trans retinoic acid at pharmacological levels overcomes repression and induces differentiation; arsenic trioxide degrades PML-RARA
ATRA plus arsenic trioxide gives high cure rates in standard-risk disease
DIC: leukaemic cells express tissue factor and release procoagulants, generating thrombin and consuming factors and platelets
Enhanced fibrinolysis (annexin II expression increases plasmin generation), lowering fibrinogen, raising D-dimer
Results: prolonged PT/APTT, low fibrinogen, thrombocytopenia, haemorrhage; early haemorrhagic death is main risk
Management: start ATRA immediately on suspicion; supportive care with platelets, cryoprecipitate/fibrinogen, FFP
Differentiation syndrome as complication of treatment (fever, respiratory distress, fluid retention); treated with corticosteroids
Confirm with cytogenetics/FISH/PCR for PML-RARA
questions.modelAnswer:
The findings point to acute promyelocytic leukaemia, a distinct subtype of acute myeloid leukaemia. The marrow is filled with abnormal promyelocytes, crowding out normal blood formation and causing anaemia, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia. The presentation is dominated by a severe coagulopathy.

The defining lesion is t(15;17), which fuses PML on chromosome 15 with the retinoic acid receptor α gene (RARA) on chromosome 17. The PML-RARA protein binds retinoic acid response elements and recruits corepressors more strongly than normal RARα. This silences genes needed for myeloid differentiation, so cells are stuck at the promyelocyte stage. It also disrupts PML nuclear bodies. The diagnosis is confirmed by FISH, karyotype or RT-PCR for PML-RARA.

Treatment targets this molecular defect. Pharmacological concentrations of all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) overcome the repression and allow the cells to mature. Arsenic trioxide promotes degradation of PML-RARA. ATRA with arsenic trioxide now cures most standard-risk patients without conventional chemotherapy. ATRA should start as soon as APL is suspected, before genetic confirmation, because early death from bleeding is the main threat. Treatment can cause differentiation syndrome (fever, breathlessness, pulmonary infiltrates, fluid retention), which is treated with corticosteroids.

The coagulopathy is disseminated intravascular coagulation with marked hyperfibrinolysis. Leukaemic promyelocytes express tissue factor and release other procoagulants, generating thrombin throughout the circulation. Clotting factors, fibrinogen and platelets are consumed, prolonging the PT and APTT. APL cells also express annexin II, which increases plasmin generation and drives excess fibrinolysis. This explains the very low fibrinogen and very high D-dimer. Consumption, fibrinolysis and thrombocytopenia from marrow failure together cause mucosal bleeding and bruising, and they carry a serious risk of intracranial haemorrhage. Supportive care replaces what has been consumed: platelet transfusion, fibrinogen (cryoprecipitate or concentrate) and fresh frozen plasma.

questions.q: Aisha, a 38-year-old woman in her first pregnancy, receives a higher-chance result for trisomy 21 from combined screening at 12 weeks. She asks what this means and what her options are. Her baby is later born with features of Down syndrome. Explain the screening pathway in England, the mechanisms that cause trisomy 21 and the influence of maternal age, and the main clinical features and associated conditions that would guide the baby's early care.
markScheme: Combined test at 11–14 weeks: nuchal translucency, PAPP-A and free β-hCG with maternal age gives a chance estimate
Higher-chance threshold (1 in 150 or greater) prompts offer of NIPT or diagnostic testing
NIPT (cell-free DNA) is highly sensitive but screening; placental mosaicism can mislead
Diagnostic: CVS (from about 11 weeks) or amniocentesis (from 15 weeks), with small miscarriage risk; informed choice and counselling
About 95% of trisomy 21 is due to non-disjunction, mostly maternal meiosis I
Maternal age effect: prolonged meiotic arrest of oocytes, weakening cohesion and recombination errors
About 4% Robertsonian translocation (karyotype parents); 1–2% mosaic
Features: hypotonia, flat facial profile, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, single palmar crease, sandal gap
Cardiac: atrioventricular septal defect (echocardiography in neonatal period)
GI: duodenal atresia, Hirschsprung disease
Other: congenital hypothyroidism, transient abnormal myelopoiesis and leukaemia risk, hearing and vision problems, atlantoaxial instability
Confirm with karyotype; multidisciplinary follow-up
questions.modelAnswer:
In England, the combined test at 11–14 weeks combines Aisha's age with nuchal translucency on ultrasound and the serum markers PAPP-A and free β-hCG. It gives a chance of trisomy 21 (and of trisomies 18 and 13), not a diagnosis. In trisomy 21, nuchal translucency and hCG tend to be raised and PAPP-A lowered. A result of 1 in 150 or greater is a higher-chance result. She would then be offered NIPT, which analyses cell-free DNA mostly derived from the placenta. NIPT is very sensitive and specific but is still a screening test, because confined placental mosaicism can cause false results. She would also be offered diagnostic testing by chorionic villus sampling (from about 11 weeks) or amniocentesis (from about 15 weeks), which carry a small risk of miscarriage. Or she may decline further testing. Non-directive counselling should support whatever she chooses.

About 95% of trisomy 21 results from non-disjunction, most often in maternal meiosis I. Oocytes stay arrested in prophase I from fetal life until ovulation, sometimes for decades. Cohesion between chromosomes weakens with time, and errors in recombination add to the risk, so chromosomes are more likely to segregate wrongly as women age. About 4% of cases are Robertsonian translocations, which are unrelated to maternal age but may be inherited, so the baby's karyotype must be checked and parents tested if a translocation is found. About 1–2% are mosaic, often with a milder phenotype.

At birth, typical features include hypotonia, a flat facial profile, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, small ears, a single palmar crease and a sandal gap. The baby's early care is guided by the associated conditions:
- Echocardiography, because about half have congenital heart disease, especially atrioventricular septal defect.
- Assessment for duodenal atresia and Hirschsprung disease.
- A full blood count to detect transient abnormal myelopoiesis, a marker of later leukaemia risk.
- Thyroid screening, and hearing and eye checks.
The paediatric team should provide long-term multidisciplinary developmental support.

questions.q: 'The timing of an insult matters more than its nature in determining the outcome of abnormal development.' Critically evaluate this statement with reference to teratogens, congenital infection and genetic causes of developmental disease.
markScheme: Embryonic periods: pre-implantation (all-or-none), embryonic weeks 3–8 (organogenesis, highest structural risk), fetal (growth and functional maturation, CNS)
Timing determines which organ is affected: critical windows (e.g. heart weeks 3–6, palate later)
Thalidomide: limb defects from narrow window of exposure (classic illustration of timing)
Rubella: first-trimester infection causes cataract, deafness, cardiac defects; later infection lower risk
ACE inhibitors: second and third trimester fetal renal damage (fetal period effect)
Nature matters: specific mechanisms (valproate and folate metabolism/HDAC; retinoids and Hox signalling; alcohol throughout pregnancy affecting brain)
Dose, genotype (maternal and fetal) and susceptibility modify effects (e.g. MTHFR, fetal alcohol variability)
Genetic causes (chromosomal aneuploidy, single-gene) are present from conception: timing concept applies only to gene expression windows
CMV and Zika: neurotropism determines brain-specific damage; timing modifies severity
Terminology: malformations (intrinsic, early), deformations (late mechanical), disruptions (destruction at any time) link timing to type
Clinical implications: preconception planning, folic acid, valproate Pregnancy Prevention Programme, rubella immunity
Balanced conclusion: timing and nature interact; neither alone is sufficient
questions.modelAnswer:
The statement draws on a classic principle of teratology: susceptibility depends on developmental stage at exposure. In the first two weeks after conception, insults tend to be all-or-none, either killing the embryo or allowing full recovery, because the cells are still totipotent. Weeks 3–8 are the embryonic period of organogenesis, when structural malformations are most likely. Each organ has its own critical window. In the fetal period, damage mainly affects growth, function and the developing brain.

The best-known examples support the claim. Thalidomide caused limb reduction defects only when taken during a narrow early window. Rubella in the first trimester often causes cataracts, deafness and cardiac defects, while infection later in pregnancy carries much lower risk. ACE inhibitors cause fetal renal damage and oligohydramnios mainly in the second and third trimesters, when the fetal kidney is working. The dysmorphology terms reflect timing too: malformations arise early in morphogenesis, while deformations come from late mechanical constraint such as oligohydramnios.

But the nature of the insult is equally important. Each agent has its own mechanism and its own tissue targets. Valproate affects folate metabolism and inhibits histone deacetylases, causing neural tube defects and neurodevelopmental disorders. Retinoids disrupt patterning signals, producing craniofacial and cardiac defects. CMV and Zika target neural progenitors, causing microcephaly. Alcohol harms the brain throughout pregnancy. Dose, and the genotypes of mother and fetus, also change outcomes, which helps explain why fetal alcohol spectrum disorder varies so much.

Genetic disease largely escapes the timing framework. Aneuploidies such as trisomy 21 and single-gene disorders are present from conception. Their effects depend on when and where the genes are expressed during development, not on an external exposure window.

Prevention reflects both factors: preconception folic acid, the valproate Pregnancy Prevention Programme and rubella immunity.

In conclusion, timing strongly influences which organ is damaged and how severely, but the nature of the insult determines the mechanism, the pattern of damage and whether there is any safe window at all. Developmental outcome reflects an interaction of agent, dose, timing and genetic susceptibility. Timing is not more important than nature in general.
